title: Easter Sunday
hook: the tomb is empty and the alleluia returns

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Easter Vigil readings, from the first light to a heart of flesh. Your line was the whole story in one night. Whose story did you tell? Day six hundred sixty-four.

For forty days a single word has been missing from every Catholic Mass. Not dropped by accident: put away. In some places, children even wrote it on a banner before Lent and buried it in the churchyard. All through Lent the Gospel was greeted with other words. Then last night, after the readings, the priest turned toward the people and sang it, three times, each time a little higher, and the people sang it back. This morning it's everywhere: on the doors, in the hymns, at the end of Mass, doubled. Easter Sunday, and the word that came back.
screen: `FORTY DAYS WITHOUT IT.` → `SUNG THREE TIMES, RISING.` → `EASTER MORNING.`

segments.voice: Start with the morning Gospel. On Easter Sunday the Church reads John. Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it's still dark and finds the stone rolled away. She runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, and the two of them race back. The younger one gets there first, looks in, and waits. Peter goes straight in and sees the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth rolled up by itself. Then the other disciple goes in, and John says he saw and believed. No angel's speech, no appearance yet. Just two out-of-breath men and an empty room. Matthew puts it in an angel's mouth, in the Douay-Rheims: "He is not here, for he is risen, as he said." Now the word. Alleluia is Hebrew: hallelu, praise, plural, all of you, and Yah, the short form of God's name. Praise the Lord, everybody. It runs all through the Psalms, and the Book of Revelation has heaven singing it. The Church buried it for Lent so that it could come back like this. Today the dismissal at the end of Mass gets a double alleluia, and it will keep it through the eight days of the octave and again at Pentecost. In many Catholic homes, Easter is also the morning of a greeting borrowed from the Christian East: one person says Christ is risen, and the other answers, he is risen indeed. The whole Christian claim sits inside that empty room. Christians say the tomb was empty because he was raised, and everything else they believe grows from that morning.
screen: `TWO DISCIPLES RACE TO THE TOMB.` · `HE SAW AND BELIEVED.` · `HALLELU-YAH: PRAISE THE LORD.` · `BURIED FOR LENT, BACK TODAY.` · then, large: `HE IS NOT HERE, FOR HE IS RISEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say he is risen to someone. First, sit for a moment and picture who it could be. A parent, a friend, someone at Mass, a group chat. Then say it, or send it, in whatever words fit: Christ is risen, or happy Easter, or simply alleluia. If you're not someone who says those words, picture the women running from the tomb, and notice what good news does to a body. The bell holds the time.
Easter Sunday. The morning of the empty tomb, the greatest feast of the Catholic year, when the alleluia comes back after Lent. Today's word.
Your line: alleluia. Praise the Lord, everybody. Today, say it out loud at least once, even quietly, even to the kitchen, for the first time in forty days. Day six hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: On Easter Sunday Catholics celebrate Mass with the Gospel of the empty tomb, sing the alleluia that was silent through Lent, end Mass with a double alleluia, and often greet each other with Christ is risen and the answer he is risen indeed.

myth: alleluia is sung at Mass all through Lent
it's put away for Lent and comes back at the Easter Vigil.
hallelu, praise, and Yah, God's name: praise the Lord.
in John's Easter Gospel, Peter reaches the tomb first
the other disciple outruns him and waits; Peter goes in first.

fork.setup: you're the younger disciple. you've outrun Peter to the tomb, and the stone is rolled away. what do you do?
options: run back to tell the others.
fork.reveal: he looks in and waits. Peter arrives and goes straight in; then the other disciple goes in, and saw, and believed.

original.note: Hebrew: praise Yah, praise the Lord — the word put away for Lent and sung again at Easter.

trapdoor: what you thought: alleluia is just a happy church word.
what it means: praise the Lord, all of you; the word the Church buries for Lent and brings back at Easter.
what a scholar hears: Hebrew hallelu-yah, a call to praise that runs through the Psalms and into Revelation.

notes: 'Burying the alleluia' banner custom: a medieval and modern custom in some places; framed as 'in some places'.
Double alleluia at the dismissal: through the Easter octave and on Pentecost (Missal); confirm.
Solemn alleluia at the Vigil intoned by the priest three times, raising the pitch; confirm.
The paschal greeting 'Christ is risen / he is risen indeed' attributed to Eastern Christian usage; confirm phrasing.
Psalm references for alleluia given in Hebrew numbering; Douay numbering differs.
